name: Flux
description: Dynamic equilibrium maintaining continuity between domains. Governs transitions between potential and kinetic states.

scope.definition: Fraction of total energy that propagates continuously through a field-coupled transition boundary (electromagnetic induction, gravitational potential, or ecosystem nutrient cycle) without conversion to thermal entropy, averaged across system types under optimal coupling conditions.

evidence.source: Faraday (1831) electromagnetic induction; Maxwell (1865) 'A Dynamical Theory of the Electromagnetic Field', Philosophical Transactions; Lindeman (1942) trophic efficiency studies; Odum (1957) Silver Springs energy budget, Ecological Monographs 27:55-112.
cross_domain_examples: electromagnetic induction: Faraday's law — time-varying B field to current with efficiency approaching 0.99 in superconductors
gravitational potential to kinetic energy: pendulum conversion ~0.99 (air resistance only loss)
ecosystem nutrient cycling: nitrogen/phosphorus flow through trophic levels 0.6-0.9
axon signal propagation: ionic flux along myelinated axon with ~0.85 signal fidelity per node
hydraulic pressure transmission: Pascal's law — near-lossless in incompressible fluids

scope.falsifiability: If a field-coupled transfer system is measured at >1.0 energy continuity ratio, it violates conservation of energy (first law of thermodynamics) — the framework fails. No such system has been found.
scope.measurement_limits: 0.92 is a system-class upper bound. Actual values range 0.6-0.99 depending on coupling efficiency and dissipation mechanism. Biological systems average 0.6-0.8. Electromagnetic systems approach 0.99 in ideal conditions. The mean masks wide variability across domains.
